checks.title: Only root has uid 0
checks.rationale: Any account with uid 0 is root under another name. Attackers add one as a backdoor because it does not show up in a list of sudo users, and it bypasses every per user restriction.
checks.fix: Remove the account, or give it a normal uid with `usermod -u` after checking what it owns.

checks.title: No login account has an empty password
checks.rationale: An account with an empty password hash and a login shell lets anyone in who can reach a login prompt, including the console and su. stackward reads the status with `passwd -S -a`, which prints a letter per account and never a hash.
checks.fix: Lock the account with `passwd -l <user>` or set a password.

checks.title: Cloud default account is locked down
checks.rationale: Cloud images create a well known first account (ubuntu, debian, admin, ec2-user), often with passwordless sudo and the provisioning key. Once you have your own admin account, the default one is a known username for attackers to target and a spare way in nobody reviews.
checks.verify: getent passwd ubuntu debian admin ec2-user; sudo grep -r NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d
checks.fix: Lock it: `passwd -l <user>`, set its shell to nologin, move its authorized_keys aside and drop its NOPASSWD line. Keep your own admin account working first.
checks.breaks: If the default account is also what your provider console or automation logs in with, locking it removes that path.

checks.title: sudoers is root owned and NOPASSWD entries are deliberate
checks.rationale: A sudoers file that anyone but root can write is a direct escalation to root. NOPASSWD entries are sometimes required (a PaaS deploy account) but are the first thing an attacker with a user shell uses, so they are listed so each one is a decision.
checks.fix: Fix ownership and mode (`chown root:root`, `chmod 0440`), validate with `visudo -cf <file>`, and keep NOPASSWD to the PaaS account.
checks.breaks: Removing a NOPASSWD line breaks whatever automation relied on it.

checks.title: Docker group has no extra members
checks.rationale: Membership of the docker group is root on the host: a member can start a container that mounts / and changes anything. Every member is listed so the access is intentional.
checks.fix: Remove users who do not need it: `gpasswd -d <user> docker`.
checks.breaks: The removed user can no longer run docker without sudo.

checks.title: Login accounts are used
checks.rationale: Login capable accounts that have not been seen for 90 days (or never) are credentials nobody watches. They keep working for whoever holds the password or key.
checks.fix: Lock unused accounts with `passwd -l <user>` or remove them.

checks.title: Root recovery path is known
checks.rationale: Whether root has a password decides your way back in when SSH keys fail: a locked root means provider console or rescue mode only. The status is printed so you know your recovery path before you need it.
checks.fix: Store the console or rescue procedure and any root password in a password manager.
